title: The Tea Round
logline: Every night for years, a volunteer has taken tea to families who have not left the hospital in days; on the night a patient finally goes home, the same round gets walked a little faster.
human_question: How do you stay useful to people's pain without either flinching from it or being flattened by it?

situation.what_happens: A volunteer makes the same round night after night, bringing tea to relatives keeping vigil while somebody they love is treated. Most of it is waiting: short exchanges, long silences, people who do not want to talk. The round does not change, but what it meets does. On some nights the news is bad. On one night somebody is discharged and goes home, and the volunteer's night is visibly different.
situation.who_is_involved: The volunteer, who has done this for years without being paid; the relatives waiting, who are exhausted and not at their best; staff whose work must not be interrupted; and patients, who are present only with their own explicit consent.
situation.what_is_at_stake: For the families, privacy at the worst time of their lives. For the volunteer, years of unremarked work suddenly being watched. For the film, the ever-present risk of using other people's fear as material. For the viewer, how a person keeps going.
situation.how_it_unfolds: A vigil has no fixed length. It runs until there is news, and the news can go either way. The volunteer's round has its own shape — preparation, circuit, refill, circuit — repeated until morning. The pressures are exhaustion, the volunteer's own life outside, and institutional permission that can be withdrawn at any time. Reality decides what happens to the family the film happens to follow, and whether the answer is good.

concept_merge.why_together: C027 states the mechanism the film is built on: compassion arises when a suffering being is in view, gladness when a happy one is, they are two different jobs, and they cannot occupy the same moment. C095 supplies the wider frame, including the failures that imitate each one — sorrow imitating compassion, giddiness imitating gladness, indifference imitating equanimity. C012 keeps the account of results honest: the volunteer is not a benefactor standing outside the flow of consequence but someone who, like everyone, both gives and receives. Together they describe a person who is not in a fixed mood but is repeatedly met by whoever is in front of them.
concept_merge.what_it_reveals: That endurance in this kind of work is not one sustained emotion but a rapid alternation, and that the tradition's test of compassion is whether it stays useful rather than whether it is felt strongly.

concept_links.why: Compassion and sympathetic joy arise only when a suffering or a happy being is actually the object, they are two different jobs, and they never occupy the same mind at the same moment [C027-P:L47; C027-M:L21; C027-M:L7].

The four abidings move from wishing someone's pain to end toward gladness at their good fortune [C095-P4:L39], and each has a failure that imitates it: sorrow for compassion, worldly giddiness for gladness [C095-P4:L47-L51]. The digest's warning is load-bearing here: the sources' own compassion exercise takes a maimed beggar as its object of contemplation, and that can never become a filmmaking method.

Rewritten after the digest check. The earlier framing of this link, years of giving whose return is not the point, rested on a line about the functional minds of fully liberated people, which does not describe a volunteer. What the digest supports is narrower and better: results are moments of experience arising from one's own earlier action with no judge involved [C012-P:L34], and everyone lives through the whole mixed range of them [C012-P:L52], so no one in this film is only a giver. Nothing about any patient's or family's situation is to be explained by their past action; the digest flags that claim as unusable.

what_the_viewer_could_understand: Compassion for someone's worry and gladness at someone's good news are two different responses that take turns, each rising for the person actually in view, so a person who serves night after night is not in one fixed mood.
what_must_be_real: Explicit, informed, revocable consent from every patient and relative shown, and no identifying detail of anyone's condition without it. Nothing about the round is arranged, and no family is followed because their outcome would suit the film.
position_hint: closing candidate: it hands the group on to the body's fragility, seen in the sick and in those keeping watch through the night, and it needs everything the group has already established about what a good mind is.
risks: High: the privacy and distress of people at a vulnerable time
Lingering on suffering for emotional effect, which the sources' own cautions rule out
Pointing a camera at sick or poor people as objects of pity, which the digest names as exactly what this series must not do
Institutional and personal consent may be withdrawn at any point, including after filming
drop_if: Hospital administration or families will not consent
Filming would disrupt patient care in any way

connections.note: Both are closing candidates handing the group on to the body's fragility, one among the sick and one among the old.
Sustained attention to one held-in-mind good thing there becomes sustained attention to people here.

selection.reason: Used by the group's closing episode; kept with its results link rewritten and its consent and dignity limits made explicit.

unknowns: No participant or event has been found or confirmed. Everything here is a research direction.
evidence_class_note: Editorial proposal. No location, scene or shot decisions are made at the idea stage.
